Female sablefish (Anoplopoma fimbria) attain a maximum recorded total length of 120 centimeters [Li = 120 centimeters], a size that reflects the species' potential for substantial somatic growth over its lifespan. This ultimate length, observed in the oldest and largest individuals within the population, is rarely achieved in the wild due to the combined pressures of fishing mortality and natural predation. In contrast, the onset of reproductive capability occurs at a considerably smaller body size; females typically reach puberty at a total length of 60.5 centimeters [Lp = 60.5 centimeters]. This size at maturity represents a critical life-history threshold, after which energy is partitioned between continued somatic expansion and the production of gametes. The difference between length at puberty and ultimate length underscores a prolonged period of adult growth, a trait common among long-lived, iteroparous marine teleosts. Field surveys and otolith-based age-length keys consistently support these length-based benchmarks, which are used by fisheries managers to set size limits that protect immature individuals and ensure a sufficient spawning stock biomass remains in the exploited population.

Under the stable thermal conditions of 2.5 °C [T = 2.5 °C], which are typical of their deep-water adult habitat, female sablefish produce approximately 2,740 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 2,740 eggs per day] through a single protracted spawning event each year [F_R_i = single protracted spawning event each year]. This daily output positions the species as a highly fecund batch spawner relative to other members of the Scorpaeniformes. The reproductive season is lengthy, with individual females releasing multiple batches of pelagic eggs over several weeks, ensuring that at least some progeny encounter favorable oceanographic conditions. This strategy compensates for the high mortality experienced during the egg and early larval stages. Temperature plays a pivotal role in governing the rate of vitellogenesis and oocyte maturation, and a value of 2.5 °C represents the thermal optimum at which maximum reproductive output has been recorded.

Early life stages in sablefish are marked by a brief incubation period followed by the emergence of a tiny, endotrophic larva. Embryos maintained at 6 °C [T = 6 °C] hatch after 14.5 days [ab = 14.5 days], a developmental duration that is typical for cold-water marine teleosts with pelagic eggs. At the moment of eclosion, the prolarva weighs just 0.0046 grams [Wwb = 0.0046 grams], a value derived from the egg diameter of 2.06 millimeters and reflecting the limited yolk reserves available for endogenous nutrition. This initial mass is remarkably small, even by marine fish standards, and it imposes a tight energetic budget on the larva before it must successfully initiate exogenous feeding. The rapid depletion of the yolk sac underscores the importance of prey availability at the time of mouth opening. The incubation temperature of 6 °C accelerates embryonic development relative to the colder temperatures that adults experience, a phenological adaptation that synchronizes hatching with the spring bloom of zooplankton prey.

Growth from the larval stage through to adulthood involves a dramatic increase in body mass. The wet weight at puberty, corresponding to the length at which females first develop mature gonads, is estimated at 2,300 grams [Wwp = 2,300 grams]. This mass, derived from an allometric length-weight relationship, represents the point at which an individual has accumulated sufficient energy reserves to support the high metabolic costs of gametogenesis and spawning migrations. Upon reaching their ultimate length, large females attain an ultimate wet weight of approximately 17,700 grams [Wwi = approximately 17,700 grams], a mass that represents a nearly four-thousand-fold increase over the weight at puberty. This continued mass gain throughout the adult phase is fueled by a piscivorous diet of forage fish and squid. The relationship between length and weight in this species follows a steep power function that reflects their robust, deep-bodied morphology. Such substantial adult body size contributes to high batch fecundity, as larger females can accommodate more developing oocytes within their coelomic cavity.

Longevity is another hallmark of the sablefish life history, with individuals exhibiting a remarkable capacity for extended survival. The maximum lifespan of Anoplopoma fimbria is estimated at approximately 94 years [am = approximately 94 years] under the thermal conditions of 2.5 °C [T = 2.5 °C] that characterize their bathypelagic environment. This extreme longevity, exceeding that of most teleost fishes, is accompanied by a slow rate of physiological senescence and a late onset of reproductive decline. Individuals may spend decades as reproductively active adults, gradually increasing their annual fecundity as body size increases with age. The cold, stable temperatures of the deep ocean are thought to contribute to this extended lifespan by reducing metabolic rate and oxidative damage accumulation. This life-history strategy, combining high fecundity, delayed maturity, and extreme longevity, makes the species particularly vulnerable to overfishing, as the removal of old, large individuals disproportionately impacts the reproductive potential of the entire stock.
